usefulness.rationale: Understanding (2): The dossier clearly establishes who Sally Kornbluth is — MIT's president — and what she has actually done: testified before Congress in December about campus antisemitism, written a note to students warning against antisemitism, retained MIT's backing after the hearing backlash, faced a House Education document request, rejected the Trump administration's higher-education compact on the grounds that scientific funding should rest on scientific merit alone, and has a pre-MIT background studying the biological signals governing cell division and death. A reader comes away with a coherent picture of the person and her recent actions, though the coverage is narrow (heavily weighted to the antisemitism/compact storyline) and omits her Duke provost tenure and academic credentials that the identity anchors reference. RemainingQuestions (1): The dossier contains no statements acknowledging what it does not know — no gaps, no dating caveats, no notes on unverified items — so it implicitly reads as complete even though major biographical segments (Duke years, PhD, how long she has been president) are absent. ConversationReadiness (2): A reader could reasonably prepare for a meeting: they would know her current role, her public positions on scientific merit and free expression, and the live controversies (House investigation, compact rejection) she is entangled in. What is missing for fuller preparation is career history and the exact timeline of her presidency. Overclaims: none found. Every dossier statement's cited quote directly supports it, including the specific-committee testimony claim (the cited article is the House Education investigation piece, so 'the committee' resolves to the House Education and Workforce Committee in context). None of the three listed unjustified conclusions (semiconductor-affiliation, initiative-authorship, birthplace) appear as statements in this dossier, so there is nothing to match them to.
